MVP case study · ConnectX

From an AI idea to a live energy product in 8 weeks

Company
ConnectX · AI building energy
Stage
Pre-seed
Timeline
8 weeks · demo in 4
Team
1 designer, 2 developers
Outcome
2 investor meetings from the week-4 demo

An AI-first energy product, scoped, proved in code and shipped by a team of 3.

ConnectX’s founder had a bold idea: let facilities, finance and sustainability teams ask about a building in plain words, and get back a working view of it, not a chat reply. Bold ideas are expensive to get wrong.

Tcules scoped the idea into 8 testable scenarios, had a coded demo running in 4 weeks and in front of investors soon after, then took it to production 4 weeks later. 1 designer, 2 developers, 8 weeks, 1 live product.

01 — The idea Week 1

A bold AI idea, and a real risk
of building the wrong thing

ConnectX’s customers were 3 very different users of the same energy system. A facilities operator needs the exception that requires action. A finance leader needs cost and a forecast. A sustainability team needs progress against a target.

The founder’s early concepts held much of the right material. What was missing was a dependable path from a person’s question to the data, the view and the action they needed.

The two obvious answers were both traps. One dashboard for everyone shows too much. A fixed dashboard per role multiplies the product, and still breaks when a situation crosses roles.

For founders

This is where most AI MVPs go wrong. “Make it adaptive” is not a spec, and building straight from the vision means months of engineering before you know whether the core interaction works.

  • SUSTAINABILITY

    Sustainability team

    Progress against an environmental target

  • FINANCE

    Finance leader

    Cost or a forecast

  • FACILITIES

    Facilities operator

    An exception that requires action

The ingredients were there. The MVP’s job was to give them a structure that responds to what a person is trying to do.

01 · The idea

02 — The riskiest call Weeks 1–2

Chat beside the dashboard, or chat that builds it? We chose both.

This was the decision that shaped the whole MVP: ship something users already understand, or something genuinely new? We shipped both, which meant lower adoption risk for a first release and a clearer story for investors.

Two directions were on the table. The first kept a conventional dashboard and added an AI assistant. Familiar, but the screen stayed the same for every question.

The second let the conversation decide what appeared on screen. It adapted more deeply, but left people nowhere to keep comparing and working with the data.

The chosen model combined both. The AI understands the question, pulls the right data and lays out the screen around it. From there, it is a normal workspace you keep working in.

The dashboard stayed, and chat became one way to build the right version of it for the work at hand.

02 · The riskiest call

03 — Scoping the MVP Weeks 1–2

We cut “an AI that can do anything” down to 8 scenarios

An interface that can assemble anything is hard to specify, hard to build and hard to trust. So the MVP didn’t try to do anything. In week 1, Tcules and ConnectX picked 8 representative situations across system status, forecasting, asset performance and operational conditions.

Each scenario was a mini-spec: the request that starts it, the intent detected, the data required, the interface modules, the twin’s behaviour and the next action available. The AI could adapt, but only within those product rules.

For founders

Scenarios turn a vague AI vision into something an engineer can build, a tester can check and an investor can watch in a demo.

Scenario areas

1 / 4

One scenario, end to end: a peak-price alert

An operator asking about a peak-price event needs more than a suggested battery action. They need to see the affected assets, the data behind the suggestion and what the action would change.

The scenario work connected the request to everything around it. That meant the information to display, the controls to offer and what the workspace should keep in place. Each scenario gave the adaptive interface a specific job.

04 — Design that ships Weeks 2–8

Design by subtraction: a simpler twin, pre-built for v1

Early directions explored detailed 3D buildings, maps and realistic representation. Realism was tempting, so the team tested it against a harder question: does it help someone understand the energy system?

The useful questions were narrower: which assets are connected, where are they, what state are they in, and which one matters now? The chosen 2.5D direction treated the twin as an explanation layer. It could highlight, dim or bring an asset into focus depending on the scenario.

The same thinking set the MVP’s scope. Generating a custom live twin for every building is complex, slow and risky to build. So for v1 the team pre-built a set of high-quality building twins, designed once and reused across customers. The product could launch on schedule, and look finished doing it.

In v1

  • 8 scenarios across 4 areas
  • The adaptive workspace: ask, assemble, keep working
  • A library of pre-built, high-quality 2.5D building twins
  • Twins that highlight, dim and focus assets for each scenario

Left for later

  • Complex, custom-built live twins for every building
  • Detailed, realistic 3D building models
  • Map views across a whole portfolio

Good MVP design removes things on purpose. Less to build, faster to ship, easier to understand.

04 · Design that ships

05 — 8 weeks to live Weeks 3–8

A coded demo in 4 weeks. Live 4 weeks later.

By week 4, ConnectX had a coded demo, not a clickable mock-up. It ran on sample data, so the founder could see a question, its data and the twin working together as one product before committing to live integrations.

That demo did its job beyond the team. It led to 2 investor meetings, with a working product on screen instead of slides.

Because the demo was real code built on the final design direction, it became the starting point for production, not a throwaway. Tcules took it through to a production module in the next 4 weeks, and it has been live since late 2025.

06 — For founders

What founders can take from the ConnectX MVP

An MVP is not a smaller version of the vision. It is the smallest product that proves the vision works, to users and to investors.

What founders can take from this

  1. 01Scope your AI into scenarios
  2. 02Build the demo in real code
  3. 03Keep the familiar, add one new thing
  4. 04Design by subtraction

ConnectX’s MVP was built to grow, not to be rebuilt. Each new question its customers bring can become 1 more scenario, with its own data, tools, view and a way back from a mistake. The product grows by adding situations it understands.

That is how we build MVPs at Tcules: a small team where design leads and engineering ships the same week, a working demo before the big build, and a first release that looks finished because what it leaves out is left out on purpose.

What the MVP delivered

  • 8 Weeks from kickoff to live
  • 2 Investor meetings from the week-4 demo
  • 3 People: 1 designer, 2 developers
  • 8 Scenarios across 4 areas
  • 60% Faster to the right view
  • 3 Pilot buildings live
  • 1200+ Questions answered in month one
  • 0 Screens thrown away between demo and production

What ConnectX’s founder says

Questions founders ask about this MVP

How long did the ConnectX MVP take?

8 weeks in total. The coded demo was ready in about 4 weeks, and the production module followed 4 weeks later. It has been live since late 2025.

Who worked on it?

A team of 3 from Tcules: 1 product designer and 2 developers, working directly with the ConnectX founder. Design and engineering moved together every week, so what was designed was what shipped.

Did Tcules only design the MVP, or build it too?

Both. Tcules defined the product, designed the interaction model and the digital twin, built a coded demo, then took that demo through to the production module that is live today.

Why a coded demo instead of a clickable prototype?

An AI product’s value is in how the question, the data and the interface work together. A coded demo showed that as one working product, convinced investors in a way slides can’t, and became the starting point for production rather than a throwaway.

What was left out of the first version?

Complex, custom-built live twins. Instead, the team pre-built a set of high-quality building twins for v1. That kept the build fast and reliable, and custom live twins stay on the roadmap.

Can you build an MVP like this for a pre-seed startup?

Yes. We start with the questions your users need answered, scope them into a small set of scenarios, prove the idea in a coded demo, then ship the MVP.
